doc.title: Doug Carn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2023

title: Whether economic circumstances shaped his music
summary: He says his music was cultural, not economic, and describes a comfortable, hustling childhood.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well that’s a good point. I wonder, the music that you created of your own, did it have something to do with what your economic situation was like?

No. No. No. It had nothing to do with that, it was just cultural you know. But see the thing is, see a lot of these musicians and athletes and other people too, they grew up, they get rich because they grew up poor you know. Now I didn’t grow up poor but I probably wasn’t far from it, especially based on today’s standards you know, but see if you grew up in a family with parents that love you and care for you and you live in a decent house, eat good food and you wear nice clothes and you drive a nice car, it might not be a Cadillac, but it’s usually brand new or almost brand new, you eat good food, you know, and you’ve got a hustle on the side. We did a lot of fishing. And then I had the band. But even when I was a kid, 8, 9 years old, I would sell soda water bottles to get a deposit you know. I kept me some change in my pocket. And then how are you going to have a four point average and be poor you know? That’s the last thing I was complaining about, that we didn’t have enough money. But I didn’t want a pony, you know, I didn’t want a horse.

But I guess if I had wanted one they would have bought me one to just stay in the stable and I could go there and ride him, but they couldn’t buy me an airplane I’m sure but I could take lessons you know, and learn how to fly you know.
